extracted.intended_audience: general readers and literary tourists interested in Shakespeare and 19th-century travel sketches
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century travel/literary-essay sketch that describes visits to Shakespeare-related sites (birthplace, grave, Lucy's Hall) and offers reflective, prescriptive remarks about how travellers and writers should receive relics, local legend, and landscape. Useful for understanding travel-writing voice and expectations of literary tourism.

rubrics_metrics.name: resolute good-humored credulity toward relics and legends
rubrics_metrics.description: The author advises travellers to be willing to believe pleasant deceptions: “I am always of easy faith in such matters, and am ever willing to be deceived where the deceit is pleasant and costs nothing. I am therefore a ready believer in relics, legends, and local anecdotes of goblins and great men, and would advise all travellers who travel for their gratification to be the same.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides travellers to prioritize enjoyment over historical scepticism; the text presents credulous reception of relics (Shakespeare’s chair, mulberry tree, yew branch) as a proper attitude for those who travel for pleasure. Anti-pattern: demanding strict factual accuracy at the expense of delight. Examples: sitting in 'Shakespeare's chair' to absorb its charm, accepting hostess’s claims unless they cost anything.

rubrics_metrics.name: overlay places with poetic/imaginative associations
rubrics_metrics.description: The author models and recommends perceiving landscapes and sites through poetic imagination: he admits he ‘surveyed the landscape through the prism of poetry’ and allowed imagined scenes (‘heard Jaques soliloquize beneath his oak; had beheld the fair Rosalind... and been once more present in spirit with fat Jack Falstaff’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a heuristic for travel writers and literary tourists, the essay endorses imaginative reconstruction—filling gaps with poetic fancy to make sites meaningful. Practical guidance: conjure scenes and characters related to the author/subject to enrich experience; accept imaginative ‘delusion’ as a legitimate pleasure. Anti-pattern: insisting on a dry, documentary account that strips places of their literary resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: use anecdote, local characters, and quotations to animate place descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator frequently incorporates local anecdotes, portraits of inhabitants (the sexton Edmonds, John Ange, the housekeeper), direct quotations, lampoons, and Shakespearean excerpts to enliven description and connect place to person and text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing technique guidance implicit in the essay: employ humanizing details, reported speech, and relevant literary quotations to give texture and authority to travel narrative. Examples in text: the sexton’s recollections of Garrick and the mulberry tree, the lampoon stanza about Lucy, quoted Shakespeare passages. Anti-pattern: dry topographical listing without human or literary context.
